methods.label: Four small squares and a sharp example
methods.explanation:
We need both a distance that is always guaranteed and an arrangement showing that no smaller distance works.

Divide the unit square into four squares of side \(1/2\). Assign any point on a dividing line to exactly one adjacent small square. Five points are assigned to four squares, so two must belong to the same small square. Their horizontal and vertical separations are each at most \(1/2\). By the Pythagorean theorem, their distance is at most
\[
\sqrt{\left(\frac12\right)^2+\left(\frac12\right)^2}
=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}.
\]
Thus \(\sqrt2/2\) always works, including when points lie on boundaries.

To show that a smaller number cannot work, place points at the four vertices and the center of the unit square. Each center-to-vertex distance is \(\sqrt2/2\). Every pair of vertices is either \(1\) or \(\sqrt2\) apart. These cover all pairs, so the smallest distance in this arrangement is exactly \(\sqrt2/2\).

Therefore the smallest universal guarantee is \(a=\sqrt2/2\), choice B.
